Leaping mullet (Chelon saliens) attains an ultimate total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters] for females, a size that positions this species among the larger members of the Mugilidae family in the northeastern Mediterranean. Field surveys conducted along the Turkish Black Sea coast and in the Sea of Azov consistently confirm this asymptotic length, which is achieved after several years of sustained growth. The species exhibits a comparatively rapid early development, with sexual maturation typically initiated once individuals reach a total length of 21.3 centimeters [Lp = 21.3 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to approximately half the maximum body size, a pattern common among iteroparous teleosts that must balance somatic investment with the onset of reproductive activity. Examination of gonadal development in captured specimens indicates that the transition to maturity is closely tied to the attainment of this specific body size, rather than to chronological age alone, although age remains an important covariate. Seasonal growth increments derived from otolith microchemistry corroborate these length-based milestones, offering a reliable framework for assessing population-level maturation schedules.

At 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the reproductive output of Chelon saliens reaches approximately 950 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 950 eggs per spawning event] during the peak spawning period in late spring, with multiple spawning events occurring over the extended season [F_R_i = multiple spawning events occurring over the extended season]. This reflects the maximum observed reproductive rate under optimal thermal conditions. Water temperature exerts a pronounced influence on gametogenic activity and spawning frequency. At the cooler end of the species' reproductive thermal window, batch intervals lengthen and per-event fecundity declines, suggesting that the 18 °C [T = 18 °C] benchmark represents a critical thermal threshold for maximal egg production. Dissections of ripe ovaries reveal asynchronous oocyte development, confirming that Leaping mullet is a multiple-batch spawner capable of releasing eggs over an extended season. The high fecundity is consistent with the species' life-history strategy as an r-selected marine migrant that colonizes coastal lagoons and estuaries, where variable environmental conditions favor high reproductive output to offset unpredictable early-life mortality.

Eggs of Leaping mullet dispersing in the water column weigh approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams], a figure consistent with estimates derived from the average diameter of 0.9 millimeters typically reported for congeneric mugilids such as Mugil cephalus. This minute wet weight at the zygote stage reflects the considerable energetic constraint imposed by a pelagic spawning strategy, in which yolk reserves must be sufficient to sustain the developing embryo through incubation yet remain small enough to maintain neutral buoyancy in turbulent surf zones. Histological examination of the fertilized ovum reveals a thin chorion and a moderately oil-rich yolk mass, adaptations that facilitate flotation and temperature-dependent developmental rates. Upon eclosion, yolk-sac larvae emerge at a similarly diminutive size and enter a brief lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. The low initial mass places a premium on rapid transition to first prey capture, as energy stores are limited and starvation occurs quickly if suitable zooplankton concentrations are not encountered within the critical window following mouth opening.

Females ultimately reach a wet body mass of 614 grams [Wwi = 614 grams] at their maximum recorded total length, a value obtained from length-weight regressions developed from a large dataset of Black Sea specimens. This asymptotic mass for females is substantially greater than that of males of equivalent length, reflecting the energetic demands of ovary production and the associated expansion of the coelomic cavity to accommodate hydrated oocytes during spawning runs. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a strong allometric trajectory, with the exponent approximating 2.97, indicating a nearly isometric scaling of body depth with length that is characteristic of fusiform, pelagic-feeding mugilids. At the onset of reproductive maturity, individuals achieve a wet body mass of 94.5 grams [Wwp = 94.5 grams], a threshold that coincides with the total length of 21.3 centimeters [Lp = 21.3 centimeters]. Achieving this mass requires approximately one to two years of growth in productive coastal habitats, a transition period during which the diet shifts from predominantly detritivorous feeding to a mix of benthic microalgae and zooplankton to support the increased metabolic demands of gonad development.

The maximum recorded lifespan of Chelon saliens under natural conditions has been documented at approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years] at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], an estimate derived from long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in the Dniester Estuary. This longevity is remarkable among mugilids and positions the Leaping mullet as one of the more durable members of the genus. The warm thermal regime in these shallow, productive estuaries accelerates metabolic processes but does not appear to shorten the ultimate lifespan, as individuals in cooler, more oligotrophic environments frequently exhibit comparable ages at death, albeit with slower growth rates. The species' extended life span is coupled with a relatively late onset of senescence, enabling repeated spawning events across multiple decades. However, the cumulative physiological toll of successive migrations between feeding and spawning grounds, combined with the gradual deterioration of fin and scale condition, eventually leads to a decline in reproductive output in the oldest age classes. Population models incorporating this maximum longevity are essential for forecasting the resilience of local stocks to fishing pressure and habitat degradation.
